The reduction in the number of ports would to a considerable extent centralize the appraisal work and place it in the hands of competent appraisers, to the great advantage of the revenue.
The royal commission, after a thorough investigation, tell us that if the number of ports were reduced there would be no detriment to

the public service, no inconvenience to the business interests, and there would be a great advantage to the revenue. I do not know whether the department has carried out this recommendation or not. If it has been carried out, and the number of ports has been reduced, then I fail to see any justification for the increase of $46,970. I presume the minister will have some explanation in reference to this point.
I desire also for a few minutes to deal with the matter of the clearance of liquor-laden vessels destined for the United States. In the debate on this subject which took place several days ago five members from this corner of the house were unanimous in their opposition to the granting of clearance to such vessels. Some of the facts adduced by the minister tended to give a rather misleading impression because some other facts in relation thereto were not stated. In general, his address might be summed up as more or less tolerating the clearance of liquor-laden vessels to the United States. One member from the subgroup on the government side also took part in that debate, and while he did not condone the clearance of such vessels he did not come out very strongly in opposition to the practice. He seemed to censure the United States for not doing all they might do. I was rather struck by the very mild tone of the speech made by the one member of the official opposition who participated in that debate. It was very much in contrast with the speech he made some three years ago on the administration of the customs department. He did not exhibit nearly the same force and vim in declaring his disapprobation of the practice of the government at this time as he did on the former occasion.
Now, the Minister of National Revenue has stated, and I think he was quite fair, that the United States government asked the Canadian government to discontinue sending reports of vessels when they were ready to clear from this side for the American side. I think that was the statement made, or something to that effect.
Only at one point, Windsor.

Well, it is quite
clear from the treaty passed in 1924 that such information could be given to the American government by our government; but we must also bear in mind that that information was given at the expense of the receiving government. The information was given by tele-

Supply-National Revenue
phone or telegram at the expense of the receiving government, the United States paying for the cost. It would look as though their asking to discontinue the submission of such information was very damaging evidence against them. But this is the point that the minister failed to make clear to the committee:	It was brought out in the conference held in Ottawa last January that in five thousand cases information had been given to the American authorities, and an investigation having been made into the said cases it was found that the names of vessels given were fictitious, the names of the owners of the vessels were fictitious, and the addresses of such owners did not exist. In five thousand cases of information sent across it was absolutely false, not because our Canadian authorities purposely sent false information but because the rum runners gave such false information to the Canadian authorities, who had no alternative except to send the information to the American authorities at the latter's expense. Can we find any fault with the American authorities for asking that such information be henceforth dispensed with? It meant an expense to them and was absolutely valueless from the standpoint of doing anything to curtail the rum running business.
Another point was mentioned by the minister, and I think perhaps he was fair in his statement. That was to the effect that not more than from 2 to 5 per cent of the liquor used in the United States was of Canadian origin. That assertion, I believe, was based on a statement made by General Andrews, who was in charge of prohibition in the United States during the year 1926. His statement' was, I believe, that not more than from 5 to 10 per cent of the total liquor was of Canadian origin. Then Major Mills, who was formerly in charge of prohibition enforcement in New York, stated that 98 per cent of the supply in the United States was produced within the borders of that country. So that I do not question the minister's statement in view of these statements made by these two gentlemen.
There is a further statement which I should like to give to the house, and this also was brought out at the conference held in Ottawa last January. The statement was made by Mr. Doran, who is now Commissioner of Prohibition in the United States, that in eighteen laboratories in the United States,
100,000	samples of seized liquor were examined in an effort to determine the origin of the liquor in such samples. I am neither
chemist nor scientist enough to know how they arrived at their conclusions as to the origin of the liquor in these samples, but I have their conclusions as given at that conference, and they stated that in the great lakes and Detroit section not over 2 per cent of the liquor in these samples related back to the industrial alcohol and other forms of control liquor in the United States. And in the New England states, in New York, in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, and in such places the figure was not more than from 10 to 15 per cent. The statement was further made that in the southwest section of the country the percentage was quite negligible. That is almost a direct contradiction of the statements made by these two other American gentlemen some years ago, General Andrews and Major Mills. I am putting this statement on record because it is just as valuable, made by a prohibition officer of the present day, as the statements tnade by prohibition officers of a previous year.
There was another statement made by the minister to the effect that the American efforts to curtail rum running were not very pronounced; that is to say, they seemed more or less to tolerate the situation as it exists. Judging from the evidence given at the conference in Ottawa, it would appear that they have been putting forth a strenuous effort. For instance, I have before me the figures in regard to the seizures that were made in the six months beginning July 1 and ending December 31, 1928. The seizures made by the American customs officers in connection with illegal shipments into the United States were these:	During that, six month period
there were 117 boats seized; 375 automobiles; 46,076 cases of beer; 4,576 cases of whiskey. The total number of seizures in that period was 2,283. I have also the figures for the two fiscal years ended June 30, 1928. During that two year period there were 634 boats seized; 964 automobiles carrying liquor from boats on the American side; 46,594 cases of beer; 6,644 barrels of beer and 16,360 cases of whiskey.
In view of these figures it would seem that our American friends have been making a considerable effort to curtail the rum running business from Canada over to the United
States.
The minister rightly stated that a good deal had been done by the Canadian officials to curtail at least the rum running business. He told us that the export docks along the
Supply-National Revenue

Windsor frontier had been reduced from forty to ten. That, perhaps, will curtail the business; at least, it will keep it within a narrower channel so that it may be more easily checked. I am not so sure that it will curtail actual shipments to any great extent. The minister also outlined the restrictions with regard to bonded warehouse.?, which warehouses are to disappear entirely ou June 11, 1930. No doubt that will have a salutory effect on the shipment of such cargoes. He pointed out also-or someone in debate pointed out-that the treaty negotiated to permit seizure within the twelve mile limit had a very beneficial effect. And by the way, I believe it came out in the conference in Ottawa that the effect of that treaty was almost entirely to eliminate rum running along the great lakes and along the seaboard. The conference held in Ottawa, to which I have made reference, was a means of airing the differences between the two countries, and while an agreement was not reached, yet perhaps we are safe in saying that some ground has been gained. But in spite of all the efforts that have been made, in spite of the conference that has been held, the business seems to be flourishing. For the year ended March 31, 1926 the value of liquor exported to the United States, upon which duty was paid, was $12,572,011. For the year ending March 31, 1928, the value was $18,380,070, showing an increase of over 46 per cent, and that represents only the liquor on which duty has been paid1; it is quite possible that a considerable quantity got across without paying duty. We also know from the debate which took place a few days ago that the government has collected through the excise tax of $9 per gallon a total of $7,800,000, and perhaps that has a considerable bearing on the attitude of the government towards this business. I am not going to make the statement that it has or has not any bearing, but it is quite possible.

I understood my hon.
friend to say a moment ago that some liquor might have gone across the border without duty being paid. Would he suggest how that could happen?
I said it was quite possible that some might have gotten over without the duty being paid. No doubt we have stills manufacturing liquor, in addition to the licensed distilleries.

They would not pay duty
anyway.

But liquor would
get across without duty being paid. Perhaps our friends in eastern Canada are so much against such an evil that they may not have stills, but I know we have had stills in western Canada which made liquor illegally.
To give my own personal point of view in regard to this matter I may state that I do not hold that Carrie Nation view which was exemplified several years ago in the United States; I am not one of those ardent prohibitionists who think if you look at liquor, smell liquor, handle liquor or even taste liquor you are going to eternal perdition. I do not hold any such views at all, ibut I do hold that the whole business is an evil tree which does not bear good fruit, I care not where it is carried on or by whom; its influence is not good. Therefore I take this opportunity of registering my protest against the practice of our Canadian government in more or less tolerating the business; I would not say we encourage it but certainly the government does tolerate it and I want to protest very definitely against that state of affairs.
The viewpoint of the United States, of course, is that they can be helped very considerably if our government will refuse clearance to these vessels, and I do not look upon that as being an unreasonable request. I am of the opinion that perhaps the Americans themselves could go a step further than they have gone as yet. I hold no brief for them; I do not say they have done all they can do; I am of the opinion that they could do very much more, and rather agree with the opinion advanced by our Canadian delegates to the conference here in Ottawa some time ago, which was to the effect that if the Americans would require registry of all vessels of every size and tonnage, that would help a great deal in curtailing the rum running business. Then they would be able to check up all their own vessels. I believe it came out at that conference that practically 100 per cent of the vessels in the business were owned by Americans.

I should like to
ask if it has not been stated within the last, few days that all these vessels are registered, just as automobiles are registered. If I might make an interjection, I would venture to

Supply-National Revenue
say that if this is the case the argument to which my hon. friend is alluding has been very much over-emphasized.

I am not sure
whether the hon. member expects the minister to answer now; I presume he will deal with that point later. The evidence brought out last January, however, was to the effect that at present vessels of five tons or under are not registered, and the reason advanced by the American delegates to that conference as to Why this was not done was that such registry would interfere to a large extent with small pleasure boats which were running back and forth. I do not attach much weight to that argument; in view of the fact that our government requires the registry of all Canadian vessels of all sizes, I see no reason why the American government could not adopt the same practice. Then we had a number of petitions presented to this house this session in connection with this question;
I have not taken time to count them but I am sure there were scores and perhaps hundreds sent in. As a matter of fact the minister himself presented petitions from different organizations calling upon the government to refuse clearance to vessels laden with liquor for the United States, but I noticed that every time he presented such a petition he had a smile on his face.
It was stated during the course of the last debate on this subject that the report of the customs committee recommended the refusal of clearances to these vessels. The royal commission, in its report, concurred in the report of the customs committee and stated that smuggling could be considerably curtailed if these clearances were refused. I think it was also stated that the Prime Minister of this country, during his election campaign of 1926, stated that he was prepared to carry out the recommendations of the royal commission to the limit. I think perhaps he obtained a great many voteg in Ontario because of that declaration and I have wondered just how many of these votes he will retain in view of the fact that he has failed to carry out what evidently was a very definite pledge to the electors of Ontario.
I am of the opinion that 'Canada would not lower herself nationally or internationally if she were to take the attitude that this business should be curtailed so far as officialdom can do it. By so doing Canada certainly would be discouraging a business which is not beneficial to the country beyond the small revenue derived from it. If we were to place on the other side of the scale the evils which come from the class of people engaged in this
business who frequent our borders and get over into Canada, such people as smugglers, gangsters, rum runners, hi-jackers and racketeers-
What is a hi-jacker?

I will have to consult a dictionary; one hon. member has suggested that he is a bad actor anyway, and I will take it for granted that he is a bad actor who is in the business for the money he may get out of it. We have such people, as well as murderers, flourishing along our borders like the proverbial green bay tree. Surely this is not a business of which our country is proud; surely after all that old Biblical statement, ''A good name is rather to be chosen than great riches," stands good to-day just as it did when it was made. That holds good for the individual as well; the individual who goes out after great riches may get them, but if he loses his good name what has he left? He has a few paltry dollars, but what good are they? The same applies to a nation, and we should take some pride in our good name. I used to take pride in the good name of Canada but I feel ashamed when I am approached and written to by individuals living in the United States who throw it up to me that we, the legislators of Canada, allow such a business to be carried on. I feel ashamed when I think of myself as being one of the legislators of this Dominion of Canada.
I take this opportunity, therefore, to register my very decided protest against this whole business. The whole business is bad and no good will come from it. The few million dollars of revenue which we obtain from it may look rather enticing, and perhaps it is enticing to the government, but I am rather of the opinion that if we did away with the business and curtailed the rough element of mankind which is flourishing along our borders, we would be moving a step forward in the retention of our good name; we would be washing our national hands clean of the whole business. The government asked for a full discussion on this matter, and I would like to urge upon them that they reconsider it. I would like to see the Americans required to register every vessel and I would like to see our Canadian government refuse a clearance to any vessel laden with liquor for the United States.

The practice of granting
clearance papers to ships engaged in smuggling liquor to the United States was discussed in this house a couple of weeks ago, but I did

not have an opportunity at that time of taking part in the debate, and I desire to take advantage of this vote to say a few words in regard to this matter. I do not want to approach the subject from the point of view of the United States, but desire simply to keep in mind the effect which this practice has upon the people of Canada. In my opinion, the smuggling of liquor is a dirty, low-down, nefarious business. The practice is made easy because we grant clearance papers to the boats engaged in the smuggling of liquor. We encourage the location in Canada of a lawless element which is a distinct liability to this country, a class of people who would kill for money, a class of people very well described in those excellent articles which appeared last winter in MacLean's Magazine. It seems to me that the practice of granting clearance papers to these ships is carried on largely for the benefit of the brewers and distillers of Canada, many of whom in past years evaded every tax which they possibly could and, in some cases, when their books were required by a royal commission, they were destroyed.
I was disappointed at the position which the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) took some days ago. He suggested that we should not stop granting these clearances to these rum runners because the United States preventive officers were not doing all they should to apprehend the law breakers. He told of how the Canadian officers notified the United States officers whenever clearence papers were granted and the boat was about to sail, and I could not help but think that it must be very interesting indeed to those Canadian customs authorities to watch the liquor smugglers dodge the American officers as well as the officers of the Ontario government. The very fact that we do notify those authorities would lead one to believe that it is an improper thing for the government to grant clearances to the boats.
That is in the treaty; that was in the agreement.

The minister said that he had limited the number of docks at which clearances would be granted, and he seemed to think that that was an improvement. I could not help thinking how much better it would be for us to prohibit clearances at all docks. The minister suggested that if we should stop granting these clearances liquor would be smuggled out of the country anyway, but that seems to be taking it for granted that the distillers, brewers and bootleggers would defy the government of the country, and that seems
[Mr. Coote.l
to me to be the wrong attitude for us to take. I do not think the minister would suggest that we should repeal the law governing the importation and sale of narcotic drugs because a lot of men engaged in that business would not obey the law. The" minister read a report made b3' one of his officers to the effect that no effort was being made by the United States preventive officers to apprehend these smugglers at one of their ports, but it is hard to harmonize that statement with the action of American officers in firing on Canadian boats and at times wounding not only the men engaged in the traffic but innocent parties as well.
I did not say that they made no effort whatever.

Possibly I should correct that and say that the minister had said that they made very little effort. However, I gathered the impression from his remarks that they were making no effort. Only a few days ago the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) made rather a long speech in which he complained about the actions of one of the United States patrol boats; that they were too zealous in performing their duty-the notorious I'm Alone case. The minister also said that he was more interested in stopping smuggling into Canada than in preventing the smuggling of liquor into the United States. It would seem to me that this granting of clearances encourages smuggling into Canada; it encourages the location in Canada of a class of men who will not hesitate to smuggle goods into Canada if they can make a dollar out of it; it encourages the location in Canada of people of the very worst type; it brings into Canada a class of people who would not hesitate to commit murder if there was sufficient money in it. This whole business is bound to have a demoralizing effect upon the people living in the areas from which the exportation of liquor is being carried on, and we are encouraging the formation in certain parts of Canada of a gangster element such as they have in Chicago. I think it is time we stopped giving official cognizance to this whole nefarious business.

I am very glad that the hon. member mentioned that matter. I have read of the same thing elsewhere, that the Department of National Revenue refused to give certain information which was asked for by the American authorities, and I desire to deny that absolutely. I will give my hon. friend information as to what we did. Under the treaty we were obligated to give certain information, and I will read the circular which was sent out by the Deputy Minister of Customs and Excise. It is dated October 30, 1926, and I may say that was very shortly before I took office. It reads:
Memorandum No. 63.
Additional instructions. 'When furnishing information with regard to vessels as provided in the above named treaty and regulations thereon, you are instructed to have such information include as far as possible the following:
(1)	Name of vessel.
(2)	Nationality of vessel.
f3) Name and residence of master.

Those were the instructions that were sent *out, and as far as I know they were faithfully carried out until at Windsor we were requested to discontinue giving that information. We sent out a further circular under date of June 20, 1927, to all the collectors as follows:
You are requested, when supplying information to United States officers under the above treaty, either by way of advance or immediate information or periodical reports to wherever possible include the particulars set out in supplement F to memorandum No. 63. This should be carefully observed.
That was very faithfully carried out. It is on record and I suppose my hon. friend has read the evidence of what took place at the conference between the officials of the two countries where our United States friends made the following statement. Admiral Bil-lard, who led the United States delegation said:
This treaty, as we all know, has not accomplished the purpose for which it was designed. In this regard, however, may I be permitted to add that Canada has fully and faithfully discharged the obligations which she assumed under the present treaty. The fact that the treaty has not tended to curb smuggling activities can in no wise be attributed to any failure on the part of your officials to perform their duties under the treaty.
If the United States authorities felt that our officers were not giving all the information that it was possible to give, why did they not accept the offer of the Canadian government to permit United States officials to come on the Canadian docks and send the reports themselves? They declined that offer.

I am more tired than I
can very well express at having to listen in the house to pussyfooting talk of this kind in regard to the subject under discussion. Surely the people of the United States are able to look after their own affairs without any assistance from us. They admit that practically ninety-seven per cent of the liquor consumed in the United States is brought in by their own people or produced in their own country, the small amount which they claim is brought in from Canada is but 2 per cent.

May I ask where
that admission is made?

I am sorry that I cannot hear my hon. friend and it does not make any great difference, as I propose to go on with my speech. We were entertained there by the mayor of the city, also by the chief of the fire department. Some of my friends whom I see before be now were regaled there with imported liquor, Johnny Walker whiskey, and other potent stimulants, dispensed by the mayor and other officials of that city.

looking at me and I deny the charge.

man in front of me who was there. That, however, is not the point. The point is that ninety per cent of the people of the United States have no intention of enforcing and do not want to enforce their own legislation. That is the real fact of the matter and I am rather tired of hearing in the house statements which in my opinion should not be made. Let the United States people skin their own skunk and enforce their own legislation. If they want restrictive laws of that character, let them enforce them. We have no obligation. We have gone far out of our way to demean ourselves in connection with enforcement of their legislation, which if they really want they cannot expect Canada to enforce. The statement made by the Minister of National Revenue the other day should have convinced any reasonable member that the government had taken every step they could in fairness or by way of international courtesy be called upon to take. Indeed I think they went perhaps too faT in their efforts to aid people to .enforce laws, many of whom say themselves they do not want enforced. But, Mr. Chairman, I want to call the attention of the minister to a matter to which I referred a year or perhaps two years ago, namely, the publication containing the customs tariff. I have under my hand a 'book of 300 odd pages. The index, instead of being printed at the beginning or at the end as in almost any other book, extends from page 129 to page 154. This publication is intitled "Office Consolidation". It is anything but a consolidation. It has been in use for twenty-one or perhaps twenty-three years. It contains appendices to the number of something like forty or fifty. There are in it schedules "A", "B", "C", "D", and I do not know how many more. There are in it items which come under two different tariff classifications and it is impossible for the ordinary man to tell under which classification some of the items come. It is a publication of which the government should be absolutely ashamed. Two years ago I appealed to the minister and also to the Minister of Finance to have some improvement made, and I remember very distinctly that they agreed with me and it was understood that some improvement would be made. There have been some slight changes made, but it is not a publication with which the government should be in any way satisfied. I appeal to the minister to have prepared a book setting forth the tariff schedules in such a way that the ordinary man can read and understand them and can see in a few minutes what the duty is on any item and the regulations in regard to it. Such a tariff is pub-[Mr. Cantley.l
lished by other countries and conditions in this country differ in no particular way from theirs. I would appeal to the minister to prepare a tariff publication properly arranged and indexed and as will be a credit to the government and the minister at the head of the department at the moment.

I do not think I would have spoken on this question had it not been, for the impression the minister gave to the country the other day. Although it might be said that a good deal is being done, and we are doing what, we can to aid the United States in the enforcement of their own laws, I do not agree with the hon. member for Pictou when he calls this kind of talk "pussyfooting." In fact, I am very glad to see, judging from the petitions that have been presented to the house from all parts of the country, that the conscience of the people is being aroused in regard to this matter. The United States have taken steps by means of a prohibition law to stamp out the liquor evil and I believe it is time Canada did the same thing. The liquor traffic is considered to be harmful even to health. During the war time we took steps to curb that evil. Since then, we have provincially tried to control the traffic, but we must admit that the result has been practically that the traffic has controlled the different governments. I think it is also true that our provincial administration of liquor laws has made prohibition in the United States very difficult to enforce. To-day we are up against a situation that calls for drastic measures. We are allowing the manufacture of the stuff, and its distribution is carried on by provincial governments. This government gives clearance to craft engaged in defying the laws of the United States. This is a difficult position to be in. The question has a moral as well as a financial side. When we give clearance to these rum-runners smuggling liquor into a country with a prohibition law we give practically a legal standing to the illicit traffic, and Canada as a nation is put in a most humiliating position as a law-breaker. At the same time we are one of the most vigorous members of the League of Nations. That is not a consistent position to occupy. I say again that it is an immoral act, and makes us all partners in what I term and what the hon. member for Southeast Grey has called a dirty business. The Minister of National Revenue says that the stuff will be imported into the United States anyway, and so far as I could gather from his argument the profits override any moral issue in which as a nation we become involved.

There is one thing certain,
that this house was given to understand that as the traffic will be carried on illegally, we might as well give clearance to these vessels and make it legal for them, and then nobody will be breaking the law. I am sorry to say that the Prime Minister himself was silent when this question was under debate in the house before, but perhaps we shall hear something from him yet. It is easy to understand from the attitude taken in this house and by the government why newspapers all over the country lauded the crew of the I'm Alone as heroes.
I want to ask, where do we stand on this question? Is it right to make this rum-running business a national undertaking, or is it not? Is Canada to follow the ideal that a Christian nation should have, or are we going to continue to break the law of a friendly country because of a profit of $9 a gallon on stuff that we ourselves have banned as a curse ?
The minister, if I understood him aright, justified the granting of clearances because the United States themselves have not done all they could to stamp out the evil. Again let me ask, are we to take advantage of a situation that gives us an excuse to comply with the wishes of a number of men who are determined to make a profit out of the depraved tastes of their fellow men and are violating the laws of a friendly country? Are we to dishonour the laws of a friendly country simply because there is money in it? When Canada dishonours the laws of another nation can we expect our own people -to obey our own laws? It is as true to-day as it was when Ilabakkuk uttered the words, that a city built and established on blood cannot last.
The liquor laws, the minister said, are in a class by themselves. No doubt they are. Too much they are viewed as if they did not have to be obeyed. The report of the royal commission on customs I think gives us the key to this line of thought. Governments through their election managers have put themselves under the power of the traffic and under the power of some of these lawbreakers. It is the saddest thing on record in our history that a supposedly valid reason for this traffic can be found by members speaking in this house to-day.
It is most inconsistent for Canada to be a member of the League of Nations and enter into a convention with other nations for the suppression of the drug traffic, and then condone law-breaking in carrying one of the worst drugs there is to a foreign country, and give clearance to craft that engage in that triffic.
I have no two standards for laws at all. I would class rum-running and! bootleggging along with murder, robbery, rape or anything else. Again let me ask, has the report of the royal commission on customs become a dead letter at this early date?' The I'm Alone incident ought to have shown us the danger into which an incident of that kind might land us. Indeed, had it not been for the quiet and steady temper of our people and the way in which they regarded this incident, I have no doubt that it might have landed us into an international difficulty of some moment. Doctor D. L. Ritchie, of Montreal, writing on the I'm Alone incident, has this to say:
The great war itself broke out when Europe's dynamite dump had an assassin's bullet fired into if from Sarajevo. How great a matter a small fire kindles, especially when primitive impulses are stirred and the baser forces of the nations set themselves to make gain out of men's follies and woes.
Again he says:
I repeat, Canada's attitude has been an example of the new patriotism, the common sense and true patriotism, a patriotism with moral standards that endeavours to keep everything in subjection to the imperial reason and confers with a nation before it begins to quarr-el.
Further:
It must be made clear that the day has one past when desperadoes can wrap themselves in any honourable flag and expect the might of which it is the symbol to hasten to their defence when caught in evil ways. Certainly to fly the British flag on anything but clean business and honourable adventure is now to soil and to degrade it; so to do must be made a crime. More and more it must wave on every breeze for justice, ordered government, and at least a measure of the golden rule.
Now, the I'm Alone incident raises questions that to my mind go to the very root of

ordered government and everything that makes for peace and good will between nations. All civilization is built on law and its observance, and the question comes down to this:	are
neighbouring states to assist each other's lawful governments or to connive at their destruction? I do not think we should talk of national honour if any untoward incidents occur while we are granting clearance to vessels manned by law-breakers who defy the laws of a neighbouring country.
Again I wish to read one short paragraph from Doctor Ritchie's statement:
We may flatter ourselves in Canada that we are not as these Americans, that our courts are clean, our police uncorrupted, our laws firmly administered and our people law-abiding. Once there was truth in all that; but are we not in danger to-day of making it an idle dream? Was not the brazen attempt of the liquor ring assisted, alas! by some of our public men, to make a hero of a rum-running scofflaw, an ugly sign of warning? And what of those in our midst, confederates of evil, who boast that they live by breaking a neighbour's laws, and are still regarded as good citizens? It was frankly asserted in one of our journals that the cargo of the I'm Alone belonged to big interests in Montreal that parade as patriotic. Why cannot they be dragged into the light? Has it not been proved that some of our brewers are behind the bootleggers? And who more swaggeringly patriotic than they?
It is a healthy kind of thing that there are at least some, journals that cannot be used to further the interests of a class of men such as those engaged in this traffic. Mr. Ritchie's article that I have been quoting will be found in the Montreal Witness. There is a real danger to-day in taking a wrong viewpoint of the public opinion created by our newspapers.
I read the other day that the Rev. Lome McTavish had declared that the four leading papers in Saskatchewan aided and abetted this work. When we see such journals upholding the crow of the I'm Alone, is it any wonder to-day that men like Harry Bronfman are untouched? In spite of the crimes named against him in the customs investigation report, that man is still unpunished. Here and now I protest against letting such men go scot free. Although the royal commission said there was a prima facie case against Bronfman, neither the Saskatchewan government nor the justice department at Ottawa hae seen fit to prosecute. As long as the illness of inspector Knowles could serve as an excuse, the Attorney-General of Saskatchewan took the responsibility for not proceeding against Bronfman. Now that gentleman says the duty is on the Minister of Justice at Ottawa, and the Minister of Justice in turn says that somebody must lay a charge against Bronfman. The charge is contained in the customs investiga-
(Mr. Evans.]
tion report, and yet this man still goes free and unmolested. Sometimes I tremble to think what a liquor-controlled press could have involved this country in had it not been for the steady character of our people at the time.
Now, unless this nation takes drastic means -and I say this in all seriousness-to curb this evil, it will as completely control all governments in Canada as it has controlled the government in Saskatchewan during the past year. Our first duty is to refuse assistance to these rum-running craft. At the conference held in Ottawa last January between our officials and officials of the United States we talked in a very friendly tone, but since then we have learned that in such a business smooth words avail very little. Admiral Billard said that as far as he could learn the aim of Canada was to further the temperance problem, but that the whole difficulty was we were handling it in a way different from that adopted by the United States, and he got the impression that the Canadian authorities seemed to think that that situation caused certain difficulties. He clarified the situation at the conference in these words:
We are asking you to consent to recommend to your government the refusal, or rather the discontinuance, of official sanction to export certain commodities into a friendly neighbouring state whose laws forbid the importation of such articles.
I take his words to be a warning. He also pointed out that- our treaty with the United States was entitled a "convention to suppress smuggling," and that he was now asking Canada to follow the policy they had already officially sanctioned. If I understood the Minister of National Revenue in this house the other day, the answer he gave to this was that we are making revenue out of this business.
Absolutely, I never made any such statement.
I apologize if it is not so, Mr. Chairman.
As a matter of fact, I was not present at the conference. I do not know Admiral Billard; I never met him in my life.

I did get that impression, but I will accept the minister's denial. When he spoke of the fact that the United States was not looking after the enforcement of its own laws, I certainly got the impression that he was inclined to let the United States look after their own laws.
Why shouldn't they?

That is all very well, but it will not excuse Canada for breaking the laws of the United States.

Perhaps that is putting it
pretty strongly; but at least we do assist the gangs that go out purposely to defy those laws.
They are not Canadians.

Admiral Billard at the conference said the only way Canada could aid the United States now would be to refuse clearance to vessels that knowingly defy the United States laws. I take that, Mr. Chairman, as a polite way of informing Canada that we are playing a two-faced game.
Now, to me it is a very serious matter. I look on it from our own national standpoint as having a most deadly effect on our young people. As for the money that is in it, I do not care how much it may be; I want law and order upheld before our young people. This is a moral question and we cannot escape it. I think it is indeed a sad reflection on our administration that since 1924 the importation of liquor into the United States from Canada has steadily increased, and Doctor Doran at the conference plainly stated that any regulatory measures would be obviously impracticable. . This border outlawry, he states, will be bound to increase. If I mistake not his meaning, he has given warning to us, and we shall have nothing ' to say if any untoward action occurs in the enforcement of that law. It may involve us yet in a nasty quarrel. I look on the I'm Alone incident as simply an incident in the prosecution of a policy which the United States authorities themselves have now adopted. I know it will be asked-have we no national pride that we allow the United States to dictate to us? They are not dictating to us. That question was put forward in this house, but I do not loo': at the matter in that light; and in answer o that I want to appeal to those in authority in Canada to-day not to put this nation, by any means whatsoever, in the position where its people will have to defend a dishonourable and disgraceful business.

I want to make a few
observations without entering into any details in regard to the question which has been thrust upon the attention of the house by hon. members to the left. That question appears to be whether Canada should or should not lend its forces at the present time
to the prevention of liquor exports into the United States. On that question I have my own opinion and conviction.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the speech made the other evening by the Minister of National Revenue and I must say that it was not convincing to me. In the efforts to grapple with what is civilization's great problem, there would be nothing wrong about the Dominion of Canada endeavouring to do something to assist in the solution of the difficulty which is being met by the United States of America. For the moment, however, I consider it far more important for us as Canadians to take an interest, a universal interest, in what we consider at present to be the solution of the problem so far as this country is concerned. Rightly or wrongly, seven provinces in this Dominion have decided that the best way to handle the liquor question in Canada is under a system of government control. I am not going to say whether I consider that the best or the worst system. All I say is that at the present time the great bulk of Canadians are of the opinion that it is the best method they know of by which to control or to cope with this great difficulty in our country. Whether in the end it will succeed or fail I do not know; but as a good Canadian, and as a citizen who desires to see a better condition of society obtain in Canada, I claim it is the business and the duty of all Canadians to give this great experiment in the Dominion the best possible chance. That we are making some headway is evident, I think, in the fact that" about three days ago the leader of the Liberal party in Ontario, who spent three or four years trying to convince that province that government control was all wrong and that some other system should be inaugurated, came to the conclusion and announced himself in favour of the government control of liquor in the provinces. Of course, he was a Liberal, and Liberals do not generally find it very difficult to turn a handspring if it suits them. And this gentleman took a big handspring and landed at this point.

Probably he was only
bringing his policy into line with the policy of this government.

No, I wish it were the
other way about; I wish this government would bring its policy into line with him. One of the difficulties which the people of Canada have had in the past to deal with this question, from a local point of view, was the fact that the government of Canada would not try to do anything to give the provinces a proper chance. With seven

of the provinces undertaking to meet the situation by means of government control- whether that system be right or wrong-what do we see taking place in Canada? The records show that we export 2,355,431 gallons of whiskey, of which 1,126,399 gallons go to the United States. This is according to the figures given by the department; and 1,229,034 gallons are exported from Canada to other countries. The other countries are classified according to exports within the British Empire and exports to foreign countries. To countries within the Empire we export 657,771 gallons, and this considerable export is largely to the small islands along the Atlantic coast. The minister knows that we export 170,000 gallons per annum to Miquelon. I see it is six o'clock and I will remain at Miquelon until we shall have had something to eat.

Miquelon, that beautiful, barren isle of the sea where liquor flows and nothing grows, and during the remainder of my remarks I wish to refer to this island as representing conditions at other points on the Atlantic ocean.
I suppose the Minister of National Revenue/-must realize that the conditions which exist on this island cannot be taken seriously; there are elements of fraud in connection with what is going on there. We will say a cargo of liquor leaves the port of Halifax and goes to Miquelon, or pretends to go to Miquelon, and a certificate is brought back to the department showing that the cargo arrived safely; the customs officer certifies that the cargo has landed and this certificate is accepted by the department as proof that the liquor has reached its proper destination, so no excise duty is charged. I understand that the government of Canada became rather suspicious of this beautiful little island and insisted that the governor of the island should also sign this certificate.
I want to point out that if this cargo really arrives at Miquelon and is unloaded at that point a duty is charged by the government of the island; in fact they charge three duties, one of which is called a customs duty, another a consuming duty and the third by some other name, but the three duties total $1 per gallon. That cargo, paying no duty in Canada and a duty of only $1 per gallon at Miquelon, has an advantage of $8 per gallon over a cargo sent to the United States or any other part of Canada, and I want to know why we charge an excise duty of SD per gallon on liquor going direct to the United States when it goes out the back door by way of Detroit or Niagara Falls and when we know it is going to the United States, with everything pointing to that fact, while if it goes out the front door and lands at this little island there is no excise duty collected. I wonder if the minister imagines that we are so devoid of intelligence in Canada as to suppose that the people of Miquelon consume all this liquor. I pointed out the other night that Canada alone sends annually over 50 gallons of liquor per capita of the adult population or 42 gallons per head when calculating every man, woman and child on the entire island. Some one says that is not enough, but I think it is quite sufficient; if all the inhabitants of that island consumed that much liquor per head for two years there would be only about two or three individuals left alive, and they would be regarded as perambulating distilleries. It is absurd; the government of Canada must know that the liquor landed on that island is not consumed there.

I am not going to discuss the question whether our excise duty on liquor going direct to the United States is too high or too low but I do claim that we should charge the same duty on liquor exported to Miquelon or to any other foreign country as we charge on liquor for home consumption, because I believe one of two things happens; either this liquor finds its way back to Canada' or it reaches some other market such as that of the United States. In any event it is objectionable. Why does the minister say that there is such a wide open door at Detroit and Niagara Falls, when we have evidence that that door is not open on the Atlantic ocean? A vessel was found two hundred or two hundred and twenty miles off the shore of the United States and a government cruiser shot it down, and yet we are told that the same government has a green light up and it is perfectly safe to smuggle liquor at Detroit and Niagara Falls. There is something a little suspicious about the statements given to this house by the minister but I do not care whether he is right or whether he is wrong, what I want to say is this: The people of several provinces of the Dominion of Canada have come to' the conclusion that they can best handle this liquor question through government control. I do not know whether they are right or whether they are wrong, but it is a great experiment and I want to say here that I ally myself with those people of Canada who are trying to eliminate drunkenness from society. This is the method which has been adopted, and I plead with this government to ally itself with those provinces which are trying to do something with regard to this liquor question. The gove|rnment should do something to help them and not leave the door wide open and thus circumvent the efforts which are being put forth by those who believe in government control. We give these smugglers an eight dollar advantage on every gallon. We are told that the smuggler and bootlegger has been eliminated from Ontario. He was eliminated when the Ontario Temperance Act first came into force and he did not reappear for two or three years, but he found out how to get around that act. In three or four years' time he will find out how to get around this government control act, and I am afraid we will have the same conditions. I believe that act is a good law but I think a fair chance should be given to the provinces to better the condition of society. No headway will be made as long as this government stands still and permits the conditions which exist at the front door of our country, which conditions only tend to circumvent the efforts being put forth by those who have faith in government control. As a Canadian I consider it of great importance that we should endeavour by every means to prevent the export of liquor to the United States. We should do that, but our greatest duty is to the people of the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, one can understand the concern in the United States about this traffic in liquor from Canada by examining the statistics. The figures show that in 1923 liquor to the value of $3,178,000 was exported from Canada to the United States. That was the legal exportation, and one can only guess as to how much was exported illegally. In 1925 the value of the exportations had risen to $11,610,000 and in 1928 the figure had grown to $24,403,000.
To come down to the particular issue which is being discussed at the present time, as to whether or not Canada should refuse to grant clearances to vessels laden with liquor for the United States, it seems to me that we are only being asked to extend a courtesy to that country which we would not for a moment refuse in our social relations with each other. I read the minister's speech of some days ago, and I take it that his opposition to carrying out the request of the United States is based on four arguments. His first argument was that we should not be asked to assist in carrying out the laws of another country. Then he claimed that the United States made no effort to curb the shipments of liquor into Canada when conditions were reversed during the war. His third argument was the obvious insincerity of the United States in enforcing her own laws, and fourthly, he doubted the efficacy of the remedy suggested by the United States, that is, for Canada to refuse clearances to vessels loaded with liquor for that country.
In my opinion, this is not an issue between what we commonly call the wets and the drys. I take it that there are tens of thousands of people in Canada who believe in government control of the sale of liquor, that is, they support what is commonly called the wet side, and yet they are in favour of the government using every means at its disposal to prevent the export of liquor into the United States. They object to Canada failing to grant what seems to be a most reasonable and modest request on the part of the United States.
The United States are not asking us to assist in enforcing their laws. In a recent issue

Supply-National Revenue
of the Toronto Star an American official is quoted as follows:
We do not want Canada to help clean up our backyard, but just to stop throwing dirt over the fence into it.
It seems to me that that covers the situation very well. He went on to say that they did not ask Canada to aid in the enforcement of their law, but they did ask Canada not to aid in the violation of it.
Every member of the house knows the difficulties a government encounters in enforcing any prohibitory law. We have heard that old cry for generations, that a government was not sincere in enforcing such and such a law. I have heard tlhe charge made in western Canada against the minister's own department, that his officers were not sincere in enforcing the Inland Revenue Act, I do not believe those charges because I think his officers are doing everything that is humanly possible to stop the illegal manufacture of liquor. Just because there are still many infractions of the American law and because the law does not absolutely prohibit the opinion is expressed that the government is not sincere in attempting to enforce the law. It is not for us to judge whether or not the government of the United States is sincere in its efforts to enforce a prohibitory law; all we have to do is to grant this reasonable request and refuse clearances to vessels loaded with liquor.
The next point in the minister's argument was that the United States had made no effort to curb shipments of liquor into Canada during the war when that country was wet and Canada was supposedly dry. I am not sure that Canada ever made any particular requests to the United States for assistance along that line, and I have no proof that if such requests were made they were ignored. But that seems to me to be a most illogical argument to use, to say that because someone committed a crime or a misdemeanor some years ago it justifies the doing of the same thing to-day. That is one of the most unsound arguments anyone could use, and I did not expect it to be used by a minister of the crown. If there has been insincerity on the part of the United States government, or on the part of their officials, in enforcing this law, then Canada is just playing into their hands, because certainly the impression is being created from one end of the United States to the other to-day that these laws are not being enforced on account of Canada's failure to grant that reasonable request. If the minister is convinced that there is that insincerity to which he refers, then he is help-

ing along and strengthening that insincerity in the United States by refusing its request. If the request were granted and there still were no particular improvements in >the situation, then the people of the United States would find out the insincerity, if any, on the part of their government.

It is a thought not consoling to our national consciousness that American thugs are able to ferry themselves across a narrow river to our Dominion and there kidnap, blackmail and arrange even for the murder of our citizens without encountering a swift and just retribution; but here are three examples of outrageous crime perpetrated within our boundaries during the past year, and in each case the guilty parties originating from the American side of the line, have been able to escape with a casual ease which cannot but be an invitation to further similar outrages.
The article continues:
It is a blazing affront to Canadian dignity, a menace to the peace and order of the Dominion, that such things as the Kennedy killing, the Williams hold-up and the Low kidnapping should go unpunished. And yet no one has been arrested.
The writer asks the question:	Why? And
he goes on to give the reason. The reason is quite obvious-the enormous profits that are made in the liquor business. I will deal with that presently. He gives many instances of men who have testified before tire commission and the various criminalities which many of them were guilty of, such as false statements, brewers falsfying their books and all that sort of thing, a story of crime and wickedness that would make any Canadian blush for shame.
In his article under date of December 15, the writer has this to say:
A geographical accident compels the peaceful, industrious and thrifty populations of Windsor, Walkerville, Ford City, Sandwich and the rest of the border towns, to accept as a close neighbour the overcrowded, cosmopolitan, rowdy metropolis of Detroit. So it came about that at the very moment that the honest burghers of the Border Cities were dusting off their palms, rolling down their sleeves and congratulating themselves that last years strenuous campaign had triumphantly routed the forces of evil which had infested .their communities for years, the worst elements among the yellow parasites who feed greedily on the illicit liquor traffic were chuckling grimly in the depths of their Detroit and border ratholes, and remarking "is that so?" Whereupon these dangerous gangsters proceeded at once to demonstrate that in this day and age, with the aid of fast automobiles, telephones and automatic pistols of deadly precision, the bloody business of murder for money is not in the least discommoded by a mere mile of smooth water.
The writers goes on:
Against the banditti of the turbulent motor city the folks of the border towns on the Canadian side are powerless. Everything that the rsidents of the Border Cities can do in their own behalf, they have done.
May I refer again to the article of January 1? He gives an instance or two to show the enormous wealth that is acquired by those engaged in the traffic. He quotes the case of Cecil Smith. He says that two years ago Cecil Smith was a taxi driver without any money. Two years after he had set up as a bootlegger, Smith boasted in open court that during the previous twelve months he had paid more than $90,000 to officials of various grades and services in return for immunity granted a score of valuable liquor cargoes smuggled across the river. In this case we have Canadian as well as United States officials bought and corrupted by these men, yet the minister assumes an attitude as if it were none of our business, as if it did not affect Canada in the least, and he refers to the United States request as one for our assistance in enforcing their laws. Surely our own law is at stake; surely law, order and decency are at stake in Canada as well in the United States. This condition is not one that is creditable either to the minister and his department or to the people of Canada as a whole.
The writer refers to the evidence given before the commission. I have not time to quote much of it, but it is most illuminating and it would be worth the while of any member of the house to read all he has to say. He gives an account of the murder of Jack Kennedy to whom I referred a little while ago. It appeal's that Jack Kennedy was an employee of a brewery on the lake front. He was an accountant and probably he was one of those gentlemen who was called upon to fake the accounts in order to defeat the minister's own officials. When he knew he was going to be called upon to testify before the commission, he suddenly disappeared. He spent part of the season in Florida, most likely under the pay of the corporation. Later on he came back to Toronto. Just a few days after he arrived there, he was served with a subpoena to appear before the court, but apparently he was a decent, honest fellow, just as good a fellow as you could get in that class of business, and he said, when asked by one of his friends what he proposed to do,

And finally listen to this. The speaker is William C. Dunford, a Canadian, and a liquor exporter of Windsor. He is giving testimony in one of the series of government actions against the brewers, in Toronto, last May. The article concludes:
How do you like that, Canadians?
Yet the minister adopts the attitude-as if it were none of our business-that it is the fault of the United States wholly when that kind of thing can go on. But I say that when a man admits in open court that he is more afraid of the thug who has threatened him than of a sentence of a judge of a Canadian court, it is not to the credit of Canadian institutions, and unless we deal with this matter we shall soon have as bad a condition in Canada as they have on the other side of the line.
What is the remedy? In a case of this kind I do not think there is any clear-cut distinction between right and wrong, or good and evil. It is a case of choosing the lesser of two evils, and to my mind the only conclusion from that standpoint, choosing the lesser of two evils, is completely to nationalize every brewery and distillery in Canada. I know that there are objections to that. Many will say that it would lead to political corruption and a certain amount of graft in connection with government. Undoubtedly there would be some graft, but certainly there would be nothing like there is to-day. The main thing is to take the private profit out of that liquor traffic, and I think that is as far as public sentiment will permit us to go at the present time. I know that consti-tional questions will be raised as to the relative rights of the provinces and the Dominion, but I suggest that the federal government take action to nationalize these breweries and distilleries. Wherever there is a province that has government liquor control and it

desires to exercise that right, let that province be allowed to do so. I think that would help to a considerable extent to clean up the situation.

Mr. Hudson points out that on account of the action of the Bahamas government the rum-running in that section has been clamped down very substantially. Surely it is not too much to suggest that the government of Canada should not be a knowing accessory to the falsehood and perjury that now characterizes the rum-running business on the border. The evidence is irrefutable that at present boats are cleared by Canadian customs officers under what they know to be a fictitious name of the boat and with what is known to be a fictitious name of the master, and to what is known to be a fictitious destination. Mr. Chairman, I should like to say one or two persuasive words in the hope that the minister will yet choose the better way. I have given this matter very careful attention and I have considered the reasons advanced by the minister and also by his officials. I maintain that anyone who impartially considers those reasons cannot say that they are impressive, except in the sense that they are unimpressive. It seems to me to be a case of alleging reasons to support a position that has been come to without the aid of reason. I am reminded of the story of the old British squire who sat down to write out his reasons against prohibition. He jotted down twelve reasons, and then to bring them to a close added a thirteenth, which read, "and for any other reason." Now. when I read the reasons that were concocted by the minister's officials after the January confabulation with the officials from the States, that story came very strongly to my mind. When I read over those eleven points, each succeeding point seemed to destroy the force of the whole case.
I think there are three very clear reasons-[DOT] not thirteen, but three-why the minister should prohibit clearances of these liquorladen vessels going to a friendly country; three reasons that stand out so spontaneously in one's mind that I would have thought they could not have been gotten around even by the official mind. The first reason is that public opinion has already expressed itself in a most articulate form in this house. In 1926 a committee of this house declared clearly that the only ethical thing to do was to prohibit these clearances. What has the minister to offset that clearly expressed will of the people of Canada? One should hardly need to bring forward any other reason. But surely if I were asked to appreciate the work of the Liberal government in the last few years I think I would say in their commendation that they had been very sensitive to the will of the House of Commons, that they had sent 
out feelers almost constantly to find out what the Commons were thinking, what they had thought, and what their position was on any given question. I would say that very freely. But here is a case where, for no adequate reason at all, the minister is going counter to the clearly expressed declaration of the House of Commons. And the onus is altogether on the minister. "But" he says, "my officials"- my officials-"considered this thing, and they outlined their reasons, and I accept their reasons." He did accept their reasons. His speech the other day was a very faithful recapitulation of the points that were drawn up by his officials. I have the greatest respect for the officials of the government. I have never yet in my contact with any of them had any cause for anything but respect But I have yet to learn that government officials in the position in which they are ought to formulate government policies on these allimportant things. They are there to carry out policies already formulated by responsible government. Do not let us hear too much about this "responsible government" business because whenever it is convenient to do so ministers and governments are prepared to shoot the whole thing to the winds. The Minister of National Revenue cannot shoulder this on to his officials, because people will immediately ask, "Where do the officials get their hunch from?" Either they got their eleven points from the minister or the minister got his eleven points from them. "Oh", you say, "well,"-and the minister actually said it -"the man in the street has pronounced on this thing. The man in the street says we have no business to try to enforce the laws of the United States."
Well, I have not much respect for the "man in the street", because I have never met him. That is one of the fictitious personages from time to time invented by people who have axes to grind in order that they might put into his mouth sentiments that would be unpopular if they came from their own lips. The man in the street indeed! He has appeared again, as he will often appear, speaking popular phrases, well-conceived catch words, that have no foundation in reason and are not meant to appeal to reason, but are meant to appeal to passion, to that ignoble passion that one nation has inherently against another. It does not matter what crisis occurs, from somewhere, from some dark corner, from some anonymous source, the man in the street, this imaginary phonograph, will get off the popular catchword-"Oh, it is not Canada's place to enforce laws in America". And that is sufficient.

The brewers of Canada are not without influence; they are not without brains; they are not without ingenuity; they are not without knowledge of this time-honoured game, the instinctive sense of psychology by which you can make use of the gullibility of the so-caEed man in the street. Someone has said that if you will let him write the songs of a nation anyone who likes may make its laws. One might also say, "Let me coin the catchwords of a party and I don't care who makes its policies"; because the catchwords will eventually rule. A very clever catchword indeed, displaying remarkable genius: It is not our business to enforce the laws of the United States-no truck or trade with the Yankees-our whole history of politics is bespattered with these despicable phrases invented by self-interest and put into the mouth of this fictitious person, the man in the street. One would have thought that a clear expression of public opinion through parliament would have given the minister his steer and not this shady and suspicious voice out of this puppet which no one knows or calls brother, the man in the street.
Another reason equally conclusive is the dictate of international good feeling. I saw on the bulletin board this afternoon that the British embassy at Washington had refused to sign any more requisitions for the importation of liquor into that embassy. That seems a small thing, and it is a small thing. But the less demonstrative a gesture the greater its value. It is not the big things that affect relationships between nations. Anyone who reads the story of the great war as told by Sir Edward Grey will discover that the things which exacerbated relations between the European nations were all despicably small things, little slights we should be ashamed almost to show between individuals. These are the seeds that eventually become dragons' teeth. If we did something openly against the United States, if we made some blatant brag, they would probably laugh at us and that would be the end of it. But no nation can afford to overlook these little courtesies and felicitations, because they are the things which ultimately determine relationships between nations. A little spark kindles a great fire and a little mustard seed will some day grow into a big tree. You may say that this is a small thing. I know it is a small thing. But when one great nation comes along to another, looks over the fence as it were and asks some small courtesy, some small concession that costs very little, it seems to me there is an opportunity we cannot afford to
overlook. But it is going to be overlooked. I think that the minister, for whose common sense and human feeling I have conceived the very highest regard, has overlooked some of the simplest impulses of our nature. I do not think the minister has ever kept chickens, for instance, on a thirty foot Lot.
Oh, oh.

There is sometimes a display
of a very inferior type of humour in this house, and I rather thought this remark would elicit it.
Who started it?

At any rate it is plain to
see that the minister was never in that situation, because he would have found out that a principle of human justice, dating back to the time when Justinian himself kept chickens, is that a man who keeps chickens must fence against them; it is not the man on the other side of the lot who must do the fencing. The man who keeps the chickens must do the fencing, and God forbid that the minister should ever keep chickens; for what is going to happen to his neighbours? Every morning the minister is going to go down when he takes the milk in and open his garden gate and shoo his chickens into his neighbour's yard; so to speak, he is going to give them clearance into his neighbour's garden. In other words, he is going to disregard a principle of justice recognized by all civilized peoples in the memory of man.
I appeal to the minister to lend an ear to such simple dictates as begot the golden rule, to such simple impulses that make for neighbourliness everywhere. The principles by which we live harmoniously together in little communities are ultimately the principles by which nations live harmoniously side by side.
I want to suggest another principle before I conclude. I think the dictates of reverence for law and order ought to have guided the minister. But the puppet in the street says it is not our business to help the Yankees to maintain law. and order. "I am not my brother's keeper" is a form of cynicism as old as 'human writing; the disavowal of any obligation for the life of our neighbour is not a new thing in the earth. But the most surprising fact is that it should find modified expression on the humane lips of the minister. It is not our business to interfere; it is not our business to help them to maintain law and order. I want to point out, however, that it is our business in a very real sense. It was Carlyle who told about a tragic occurrence in a Scottish city, when some poor people caught the typhus fever in the slums

of that city. The wealthy people in the west end said, "That is not our business; they must look after themselves." But the typhus germ, being a veiy democratic animal, did not stay in the slums; it strayed over into the other end of the city and the city was decimated. Now that is what is going to happen on our border if we disavow responsibility for helping the United States to maintain law and order. If we refuse to recognize that responsibility, do you think we are going to be able to stem the flood of lawlessness and disorder that will break through that invisible line? I do not think we can expect it.
We have heard a good deal this session about the tragedy of divorce, the breaking up of homes. You know that homes do not break up spontaneously; all kinds of moral influences contribute to that result. Do you think these influences can be stopped at the border? Do you think that by talking about divorce or social ethics in this house you are going to put up an insuperable barrier at the border? That cannot be done in that way, but it can be done by showing some sincere effort to maintain social conditions, not only here but on the other side of the line as well which will lend themselves to the establishment of our old-time institutions. No, we cannot be indifferent to what is going on across the line; sooner or later our homes will be exposed to the same influences.
In closing I want to remind hon. gentlemen that this house spoke two or three years ago, and as far as I can learn no one has spoken since except the "man in the street," who does not exist. The dictates of international good feeling implore my hon. friend to take a different course; respect for law and order on both sides of the line also pleads with him to yield this simple point, which will cost Canada practically nothing. He is asked simply to place his prohibition on the clearance of these vessels.

I do not 'want to prolong the debate or take up the time of the house unnecessarily, but I should like to add a word or two to this discussion. During the days of the Drury government in Ontario it was a popular pastime to picture the border along the Detroit river as a terrible place and the people who lived there as outlaws; it used to be suggested that it would not be safe for decent or respectable people to walk the streets after dark, and apparently some of our hon. friends in the southeast comer have caught the fever. I would like

to tell them that the distillers, the brewers and the exporters are doing an honest business and are living up to the law. Whenever churches, hospitals and other charitable institutions want help they do not forget to call upon these people for money, and they are usually very generous in responding.
With regard to the articles in the Toronto Star and in MacLean's magazine, I want to say that these articles are written in the most sensational manner possible. In order to illustrate the unfairness of the Toronto Star I might tell the committee that prior to the last election they sent to the border a couple of reporters who laid indiscriminate charges against four exporters in East Essex, four in West Essex and two breweries, but when the magistrate called the cases the next day these men were not to be found; they had gone over the river. After the election was over the cases proceeded, with the result that these men had not a tittle of evidence to support their charges, and they received a severe reprimand from the magistrate.
I am firmly of the opinion that it is not up to Canada to attempt to enforce the Volstead act of the United States, a law which they themselves make very little attempt to enforce. For instance, when the river was frozen over and the boats could not cross, all through the day there was a long stream of automobiles and sleighs carrying goods across the river below Ojibway from the Canadian side to Detroit, and hundreds of people watched them unload and reload their cargoes in broad daylight.
Hon. gentlemen spoke about these thugs and bootleggers and implied that they were Canadians, but that is not the fact. Last fall they had an investigation on the American side and discharged about one hundred or more preventive officers, many of whom were found to be criminals themselves; some-of them were house-breakers,, thieves and hijackers. I was very much amused at the reference by the hon. member for Kinders-ley as to the number of automobiles that had been seized. [DOT] They may seize an occasional automobile in Detroit, which is sent to the police department to be sold; a friend of the bootlegger usually buys back the car for $5 or $10, and that is all there is to it. A number of boats were seized and taken to>
anchorage, and when the time came to sell them it was discovered that they had all disappeared.
I claim that if the United States officials were in earnest they could stop the bootlegging across the Detroit river, but they are not in.
