earnest. I also think the United States owes Canada a debt of gratitude for allowing their bootleggers to import this liquor; if they were not able to get a supply of good liquor and beer their people would be drinking squirrel whiskey and all that sort of stuff, which sends them to the hospital and blinds them, as had happened in a hundred cases, especially a few years ago. I do not know that I have anything further to say except to add that I am heartily in accord with the statement made by the minister a few days ago.

Like the hon. member for West Essex I do not wish to prolong the debate, but I do wish to say that I agree with very much of the statement the minister made in the house a few days ago, and my chief reason for taking this attitude is that I believe the minister and his department have more than they can handle in enforcing the Canadian laws with regard to liquor.
I did not rise to hand out any compliments; I am going to criticize the department, because I believe their decision of a few months ago to close a number of preventive stations and outports in the maritime provinces will make a paradise out of what was formerly a garden of eden for the smugglers. I need scarcely say that when vessels were obliged to enter and clear at the different ports, the department had a close check upon them; they were able to follow the course of these vessels from day to day and from week to week, and they knew pretty well what was going on. The present plan is that all coastwise vessels may enter and leave these ports freely, without the necessity of either entering or clearing. What will be the result? Look at the advantage it will be to the smugglers if they are not obliged to report anywhere during the whole season, if they do not choose to do so; they can go into and out of practically all the different rivers and harbours of Prince Edward Island; they can go out to the gulf and meet the mother ship loaded with liquor and return to any of these harbours openly and freely. So I say the department has done more to assist the smuggler than can be overcome by any means at its disposal.
I have a further complaint to make with regard to the closing of these offices; I refer to the inconvenience this action will cause a great many people in many sections of the country. I believe the minister has received a petition signed by a large number of the residents of one of the ports where the office was closed, and as it is short and concise I will read it in order to show in some measure
the inconvenience these people will suffer as a result of this action. This petition is addressed to the hon. minister, and reads as follows:
The undersigned residents of Cardigan and vicinity, in the county of Kings, Prince Edward Island, having learned that your department proposes to close the customs office in the village of Cardigan, take the liberty of making the following representations in connection therewith.
(1)	This office has been an established institution since the province joined confederation, and is a very great convenience to the people of a large and prosperous section of country.
(2)	The village of Cardigan is the customs and railway centre shipping port for a number of large and populous settlements, some of which are twelve to fifteen miles from the railway, and all of which will be seriously inconvenienced by the closing of this office.
(3)	The entering and clearing of vessels is a matter of much importance, and while this does not bring in revenue, and we realize that the office may not be profitable from that standpoint, we beg to submit that the service given to the public generally is so great as to more than justify its maintenance in view of the very small salary and expense connected with it.
(4)	In stressing the urgency of this matter we wish to represent that the question of revenue should not be the department's only guide in such cases. Accommodation to the public is being given in most branches of government service without regard to financial returns, and we believe this is a case in which the needs of a large section of country should be considered rather than the small economy which can be effected by closing the office.
Therefore we earnestly pray that your department should give further consideration to this case, and trust you may see your way clear to meet our views, and the needs of this district, by maintaining the customs office at Cardigan.
The same arguments could be applied to several other districts where the offices have been closed, notably at Murray Harbour, Murray River, and St. Peter's Bay, and to a lesser extent at Annandale. During the summer time there is a considerable traffic from the United States to Prince Edward Island. Many of our people who have gone to that country to work return for a visit to their friends, and of course the custom is to check their baggage through from Boston or New York, or whatever point they depart from. Take the case of Cardigan. A man writes to his friends at that point advising them that he expects to arrive 'by a certain train, and he checks his baggage through. Perhaps his friends have to drive twelve or fifteen miles to meet him, and then it is discovered that they cannot get his baggage. What axe they going to do about that? They will have to go back home and make another trip to some other place where there is a customs house in order to have the baggage examined. Considerable hardship will be caused through

closing this office, when it could be averted by continuing to pay the small salary which was paid to the official at that point. The reason given is that the customs returns have been so small, but if the same principle were applied to other branches of the government service many offices would have to be closed. It would be found necesasry to close most of the post offices if they were considered on a revenue basis.
There is another port which I would like to mention, the port of Georgetown. This is the winter port of Prince Edward Island, and is the port of call for many vessels. I have made representations both -to the minister and to the commissioner of customs regarding this matter. I made them as strong as I could, and I wish to repeat them here. The only expense at that port is the salary of the official, because there is a government building which houses both the customs and the post office. That building has to be maintained, heated and lighted for the post office, regardless of whether or not the customs house is maintained. This customs office was established long before confederation.
